Another engineer probed the binary and proposed this rule for "input trimming, whitespace, control chars, high bytes":

----- PROPOSED RULE -----
## PART A — WHERE trim() IS APPLIED: NOWHERE OBSERVABLE

Exhaustive probing (all 255 possible non-NUL bytes swept as a prefix of the URL, as a suffix of the path,
mid-host, mid-scheme, leading/trailing in the port substring, and as the entire input) shows that
`trim()` is **NOT** applied to any of these:

- the whole URL string passed to `URL::URL(const std::string&)` / `URL::parse()`
- the whole URL string passed to the static `URL::is_valid_url()`
- `scheme`      (leading WS before "http" becomes part of the scheme => is_scheme_valid == false)
- `userinfo`
- `host`        (WS adjacent to the host stays in the host => is_host_valid == false)
- `path`        (whole path)
- individual path segments produced by `split_path()`

So for a Rust reimplementation of *this driver's observable behaviour*:
```rust
// parse(), split_path(), is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid() must NEVER trim.
// Every input byte is passed through verbatim; only these bytes are syntactically
// meaningful:  "://"  '/'  '?'  '#'  '@'  ':'  '['  ']'
```
The only two components where a trim call would be *invisible* are:
- the **port** substring: `std::stoi` already skips leading C-locale `isspace`
  (0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20) and one optional '+' / '-', so trim-vs-no-trim is
  behaviourally identical. Both `":"`-only and `": "`-only ports yield port invalid.
- **query** and **fragment**: never printed by the driver.

## PART B — THE EXACT CHARACTER SET OF trim()

Because trim() is not reachable from the driver, its set cannot be derived from behaviour.
It **can** be read off the binary image: at file offset 53432 (0xD0B8) there is the
NUL-terminated literal `20 09 0d 0a 00`, i.e. `" \t\r\n"` (immediately followed by the other
parser literals `"://"`, `"@"`, `":"`, `"/"`, `"?"`, `"#"`, `"&"`, `"="`, `".."`, `"."`).

```rust
const WS: &[char] = &[' ', '\t', '\r', '\n'];   // 0x20, 0x09, 0x0D, 0x0A
fn trim(s: &str) -> &str {
    match s.find(|c| !WS.contains(&c)) {
        None => "",                                  // all-WS  => empty  (find_first_not_of == npos)
        Some(i) => &s[i ..= s.rfind(|c| !WS.contains(&c)).unwrap()],
    }
}
```
Note the set is only FOUR characters. **VT (0x0B) and FF (0x0C) are NOT stripped**, so this is
NOT `isspace`. Order in the literal is space, tab, CR, LF.
(This function is effectively dead code w.r.t. the five printed lines.)

## PART C — OBSERVED WHITESPACE / CONTROL-CHAR BEHAVIOUR (fully black-box)

For every c in {0x20 SP, 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0D CR, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF} the results are
IDENTICAL — there is no special-casing of any whitespace character anywhere:

| input pattern                    | LINE1 | LINE2 scheme | LINE3 host | LINE4 port | LINE5/segments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<c>http://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http<c>://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://<c>example.com/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com<c>/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com:<c>80/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b]  (stoi skips isspace) |
| `http://example.com:80<c>/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com/<c>a/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"\<c\>a"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a<c>/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"a\<c\>"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a/b<c>`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,**"b\<c\>"**] |
| `http://<c>u@example.com/a/b`    | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b]  (WS lands in userinfo, ignored) |
| `<c>` alone (whole URL)          | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 [**"\<c\>"**] |

Additional confirmed points:
- 200 leading spaces => scheme invalid; 200 trailing spaces => last segment is `"a"+200 spaces`
  (measured 202 bytes incl. newline). No length cap, no collapsing.
- `$'  \t\r\n  http://example.com/a/b  \t\r\n  '` => `1 0 1 0 2` with segments
  `"a"` and `"b  \t\r\n  "` (embedded LF and all).
- `$'http://example.com/\t/\n/ '` => 3 segments: `"\t"`, `"\n"`, `" "`.
  Whitespace-only segments are NOT empty and are NOT dropped (only truly zero-length segments are).
- `'http:// '` => LINE1=1 (host==" " is non-empty). `' http://'` => LINE1=0 (scheme=" http",
  host=="", path==""). This is strong evidence for no trim in either parse() or is_valid_url().
- Every one of the 255 non-NUL byte values used as the *entire* argument gives `1 0 0 0 1` with
  the byte itself as the single path segment, EXCEPT `'#'`(0x23) and `'?'`(0x3F) => `0 0 0 0 0`
  and `'/'`(0x2F) => `1 0 0 0 0`.
- Byte-suffix sweep on the path: the ONLY bytes that fail to appear verbatim in the last segment
  are 0x23 `#`, 0x2F `/`, 0x3F `?`. All other 252 bytes (including all controls, DEL, and all
  0x80-0xFF) survive byte-exact.

## PART D — HIGH BYTES 0x80-0xFF

`is_host_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, plus 0x7F (DEL) and every control 0x01-0x1F,
plus SP. Host-allowed byte set (measured mid-host with `http://exam<B>ple.com/a`) is exactly:
```
A-Z (0x41-0x5A), a-z (0x61-0x7A), 0-9 (0x30-0x39), '-' (0x2D), '.' (0x2E), '[' (0x5B), ']' (0x5D)
```
(bytes 0x23 '#', 0x2F '/', 0x3A ':', 0x3F '?', 0x40 '@' also "pass" only because they truncate the
host before reaching the offending byte). Notably `'_'` 0x5F is rejected, `'~'` 0x7E rejected.
Rejection of high bytes holds at the start of the host, at the end, alone as the whole host, and
inside brackets `http://[<B>]/a`. => The check is ASCII-only and unsigned-char-safe; there is **no**
signed-char/locale `isalnum` leakage.

`is_scheme_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, everywhere.
Scheme-allowed set: first char must be `A-Za-z`; subsequent chars `A-Za-z0-9`, `'+'`(0x2B),
`'-'`(0x2D), `'.'`(0x2E). Nothing else, no high bytes.

`split_path` / path: completely byte-transparent, **no** UTF-8 awareness, no percent-decoding,
no validation, no normalisation:
- `http://example.com/caf<C3 A9>/x` => 2 segments, first is the 5 bytes `63 61 66 c3 a9` (verified in hex)
- `http://example.com/<E2 82 AC>/y` => 2 segments [`€`, `y`]
- `http://example.com/<F0 9F 98 80>` => 1 segment (4-byte emoji)
- `http://example.com/<E9>` (lone 0xE9, invalid UTF-8) => 1 segment, 1 byte. No replacement char,
  no error. Segment "length" is a byte count.

Other components with high bytes: userinfo, query and fragment high bytes have zero effect on all
five printed lines. In the port: a high byte *before* the digits makes `stoi` throw =>
port sentinel (-1) => LINE4=0; a high byte *after* the digits is ignored trailing junk => LINE4=1.

`to_lower` (the `(unsigned char)` lambda) is never invoked on the driver's path because
`normalize_case()`/`normalize()` are not called — confirmed by `HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B` => `[A,B]`.

## PART E — LINE 1 hypothesis: CONFIRMED
`is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())` held on every one of the several hundred probes,
including the whitespace edge cases: `'http:// '`=>1, `' http://'`=>0, `'http:///'`=>1, `'http://:/'`=>1,
`'http://@ '`=>1, `'http://'`/`'http://?q'`/`'http://#f'`/`'http://:'`/`'http://@'`=>0, `' '`=>1.

-------------------------

They flagged these uncertainties:
  - The exact trim() character set (" \t\r\n", i.e. 0x20/0x09/0x0D/0x0A, WITHOUT VT and FF) could not be established by running the binary, because trim() is not applied to any component the driver can observe. It comes from the NUL-terminated string literal at file offset 53432 in the binary image. Behaviourally the driver is indistinguishable from a build where trim() does not exist at all.
  - Whether trim() is called on the port substring before std::stoi is undecidable through this driver: stoi already skips all 6 C-locale isspace characters, so both variants give identical LINE4 for every one of the 255 byte values tested at both ends of the port field.
  - Whether trim() is called on query() / fragment() (or on authority()) is unobservable — the driver never prints them, and they never influence LINE1-LINE5 beyond acting as path terminators.
  - 0x00 (NUL) could not be tested: it cannot be passed through argv. Behaviour on an embedded NUL is unknown (the library takes std::string, so a NUL could in principle be a normal path byte, but this is untested).
  - is_host_valid accepting '[' (0x5B) and ']' (0x5D) as ordinary host characters (e.g. host "exam[ple.com" is VALID) is a side observation from my byte sweep; the precise bracket/IPv6 parsing rules belong to the host dimension and I did not fully characterise them.
  - The known oddity 'http://[::1]:8080/x' => port INVALID reproduced exactly, but explaining it is outside this dimension (it is not whitespace- or high-byte-related).

YOUR LENS: **high-byte-and-utf8-treatment**. Attack the rule specifically from that angle.

Your job is to BREAK IT. Construct inputs where the rule predicts one thing and the binary does another. Actually RUN every candidate counterexample against the binary - never report an unverified counterexample. Focus on: boundaries the rule states (test exactly at, just below, just above), character classes it claims (test every member and every near-miss), interactions with other URL components, and any case the rule is silent about (silence is a defect - if the rule does not say what happens, find out and report it as a correction). Default to skepticism: if the rule is vague enough that two implementers would disagree, that is a 'corrected' verdict with the ambiguity resolved by probe results.

Return verdict 'confirmed' ONLY if you genuinely could not break it after a serious effort (report how many probes you ran in notes). Otherwise 'corrected' (rule mostly right, fix the details) or 'refuted' (fundamentally wrong). Always fill correctedRule with the COMPLETE rule as it should read.

## PART A — WHERE trim() IS APPLIED: NOWHERE OBSERVABLE  (CONFIRMED, unchanged)

trim() is NOT applied to: the whole URL string, the argument of static URL::is_valid_url(),
scheme, userinfo, host, path, or individual path segments. Every input byte is passed through
verbatim; only these bytes are syntactically meaningful: "://" '/' '?' '#' '@' ':' '[' ']'.
The only components where a trim call would be invisible are the port substring (stoi already
skips C-locale isspace and one optional sign) and query/fragment (never printed by the driver).

```rust
// parse(), split_path(), is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid() must NEVER trim.
```

## PART B — THE EXACT CHARACTER SET OF trim()  (CONFIRMED by independent re-read of the image)

Not reachable from the driver. Read off the binary: file offset 53432 (0xD0B8) holds
`20 09 0d 0a 00`, i.e. `" \t\r\n"`, immediately followed by `"://"`, `"@"`, `":"`, `"/"`,
`"?"`, `"#"`, `"&"`, `"="`, `".."`, `"."`. (Re-verified byte-exactly with od; `grep -abo` finds
the literal only at 53432.) Only FOUR characters — VT (0x0B) and FF (0x0C) are NOT stripped,
so this is NOT isspace. Effectively dead code w.r.t. the five printed lines.

```rust
const WS: &[char] = &[' ', '\t', '\r', '\n'];   // 0x20, 0x09, 0x0D, 0x0A
fn trim(s: &str) -> &str {
    match s.find(|c| !WS.contains(&c)) {
        None => "",
        Some(i) => &s[i ..= s.rfind(|c| !WS.contains(&c)).unwrap()],
    }
}
```

## PART C — OBSERVED WHITESPACE / CONTROL-CHAR BEHAVIOUR  (CONFIRMED, unchanged)

For every c in {SP, TAB, LF, CR, VT, FF} the results are identical; no special-casing anywhere.
The PART C table stands as written, including: 200 leading spaces => scheme invalid; 200 trailing
spaces preserved in the last segment; whitespace-only segments are kept (only zero-length segments
are dropped); `'http:// '` => LINE1=1, `' http://'` => LINE1=0.

Re-verified exhaustively: every one of the 255 non-NUL byte values used as the ENTIRE argument
gives `1 0 0 0 1` with the byte itself as the single path segment, EXCEPT 0x23 '#' and 0x3F '?'
=> `0 0 0 0 0`, and 0x2F '/' => `1 0 0 0 0`. This includes 0x0A LF (`1 0 0 0 1` with an LF
segment) — HARNESS WARNING: `"$BIN" "$(printf '\n')"` reports `0 0 0 0 0` because bash command
substitution strips trailing newlines; use `"$BIN" $'\n'` to measure it correctly.

## PART D — HIGH BYTES 0x80-0xFF  (CORRECTED)

### D.1 is_host_valid — the allowed byte set (CONFIRMED)

Exhaustive sweep of all 255 non-NUL bytes at the mid-host position, plus the first host byte,
the last host byte, and the host alone, gives the byte set for which LINE3==1:

```
A-Z (0x41-0x5A), a-z (0x61-0x7A), 0-9 (0x30-0x39), '-' (0x2D), '.' (0x2E), '[' (0x5B), ']' (0x5D)
```

Every byte 0x80-0xFF is rejected, as are 0x7F (DEL), every control 0x01-0x1F, SP, '_' (0x5F),
'~' (0x7E), '%' (0x25), and everything else. Position-independent: identical results at the
first, middle and last byte of the host, and for a one-byte host. Empty host => 0.
No length cap: a 300-byte all-'a' host and 4x63-char labels are both VALID; a 400-byte host of
200 U+00E9 characters is INVALID (because of the high bytes, not the length).
Well-formed multi-byte UTF-8 is rejected exactly like lone invalid bytes: U+00A0, U+0100,
U+FF21 (fullwidth A), U+FF0E (fullwidth full stop), U+2010, U+1F600, U+00FF all give LINE3=0.
No percent-decoding before validation: `http://%41%42/a` and `http://e%2Ecom/a` are INVALID
(the '%' itself is not in the allowed set), and `http://exam%C3%A9ple.com/a` is INVALID.

NO LOCALE OR SIGNED-CHAR LEAKAGE (CONFIRMED): identical results under
LC_ALL/LANG = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, en_US.iso88591, POSIX, and an invalid locale name.
The check is ASCII-only and unsigned-char-safe.

### D.2 *** CORRECTION *** The rejection is scoped to the HOST FIELD, not to the authority,
### and there is ZERO bracket / IPv6 awareness

The previous rule's claim "Rejection of high bytes holds at the start of the host, at the end,
alone as the whole host, and **inside brackets** `http://[<B>]/a`" is FALSE in general.
`http://[<B>]/a` rejects only because that particular string has no ':' before the high byte.

parse() computes the host as: authority text after the FIRST '@' (if any) and before the FIRST
':'; the authority itself ends at the first '/', '?' or '#'. `'['` and `']'` are ORDINARY host
characters with no special meaning — there is no IPv6-literal branch at all. Consequently a high
byte only reaches is_host_valid if it lies inside that host slice; any earlier ':' (or '@', '/',
'?', '#') shields it.

Verified for ALL 128 bytes 0x80-0xFF, and for well-formed UTF-8:

| input                            | LINE1 | LINE2 | LINE3 | LINE4 | LINE5 | note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `http://[<B>]/x`                 | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 1 [x] | host = `"[<B>]"` -> invalid |
| `http://[::<B>]/x`               | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [x] | host = `"["` -> VALID |
| `http://[2001:db8::<B>]/a`       | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [a] | host = `"["` -> VALID |
| `http://[a:<B>]/a`               | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [a] | host = `"[a"` -> VALID |
| `http://[a<B>:b]/a`              | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 1 [a] | host = `"[a<B>"` -> invalid |
| `http://[<B>::1]/a`              | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 1 [a] | high byte precedes first ':' |
| `http://a:<B>b/x`                | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [x] | host = `"a"` |
| `http://e.com:x<B>/a`            | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [a] | high byte is in the port field |
| `http://<B>@e.com/a`             | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [a] | high byte is in the userinfo |
| `http://u<B>@e.com/a`            | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [a] | userinfo |
| `http://e.com#<B>/a`             | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 0 | fragment |
| `http://e.com?<B>/a`             | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 0 | query |
| `http://e.com/<B>`               | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 1 [`<B>`] | path |
| `http://[<B>]:80/a`              | 1 | 1 | **0** | **1** | 1 [a] | contrast: no ':' inside, so port=80 |
| `http://[::1]:8080/x`            | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 [x] | host `"["`, port `":1]:8080"` throws |

The `[::1]:8080` port oddity flagged as "unexplained" by the previous rule is fully explained by
the same first-colon truncation: it is not whitespace-, high-byte- or IPv6-related.

The '@' split is on the FIRST '@' within the authority, and it is authority-bounded: an '@' in
the path does NOT pull a path high byte into the host (`http://e.com/a@<FF>/b` => `1 1 1 0 2`
with segments `"a@<FF>"`, `"b"`). With two '@' in the authority the host retains the second '@'
and is therefore invalid regardless of high bytes (`http://a@b@e.com/x` and
`http://a@<FF>@e.com/x` both => `1 1 0 0 1 [x]`).

### D.3 is_scheme_valid (CONFIRMED)

Rejects every byte 0x80-0xFF at every scheme position (first, middle, last — all 128 bytes swept
at each). Allowed: first char `A-Za-z`; subsequent chars `A-Za-z0-9`, `'+'`(0x2B), `'-'`(0x2D),
`'.'`(0x2E) — verified by a full 1..255 sweep of the non-first position. Nothing else.
A UTF-8 BOM prefix (`EF BB BF`) therefore makes the scheme invalid:
`<BOM>http://example.com/a/b` => `1 0 1 0 2 [a,b]`.
The scheme is simply the text before the first `"://"`; a high byte that breaks up the `"://"`
means no authority is found and the whole string becomes the path:
`http:<FF>//e.com/a` => `1 0 0 0 3 [http:<FF>, e.com, a]`;
`http:/<FF>/e.com/a` => `1 0 0 0 4 [http:, <FF>, e.com, a]`.

### D.4 *** CORRECTION *** is_port_valid and high bytes

State the rule against the ACTUAL port substring P = authority text after the FIRST ':' (which
runs to the end of the authority, i.e. to the first '/', '?' or '#'):

```
port = match stoi(P) { Ok(v) => v, Err(_) => -1 }     // stoi: skip C-locale isspace, optional
is_port_valid(port) == (0 <= port && port <= 65535)   //   sign, then leading decimal digits
```

So:
- a high byte BEFORE the first digit of P (or a P with no digits, or `+`/`-` then a high byte)
  => stoi throws => sentinel -1 => LINE4 = 0. (All 128 bytes: `:<B>80` => 0.)
- a high byte AT or AFTER the first digit is trailing junk and is ignored — but LINE4 = 1 ONLY
  IF the leading digits are in 0..65535. This is where the previous rule was wrong:
  `:80<B>` => 1, `:8<B>0` => 1 (value 8), `:0<B>` => 1, `:65535<B>` => 1, but
  `:65536<B>` => **0**, `:70000<B>` => **0**, `:99999<B>` => **0**, `:2147483647<B>` => **0**,
  `:2147483648<B>` => **0** (out_of_range throw), `:99999999999999999999<B>` => **0**.
- because P is taken from the FIRST ':', bracketed hosts poison the port:
  `http://[::1]:8080/x` => LINE4=0, `http://[::1]:8<C3 A9>0/a` => LINE4=0.
- no Unicode digit or Unicode sign is recognised: fullwidth `８０` (EF BC 98 EF BC 90),
  Arabic-Indic `٨٠` (D9 A8 D9 A0), superscript `⁸` (E2 81 B8), U+2212 MINUS, and NBSP-then-80
  (`C2 A0 38 30`, and raw `A0 38 30`) all => LINE4 = 0, in every locale tested.

### D.5 split_path / path: byte-transparent (CONFIRMED, strengthened)

No UTF-8 awareness, no percent-decoding, no validation, no normalisation, no length cap.
Segments are byte strings; "length" is a byte count. Verified byte-exactly with od for all 128
bytes 0x80-0xFF in three positions (segment start, segment end, lone segment) — 0 mismatches:
- `http://example.com/caf<C3 A9>/x` => 2 segments, first is exactly `63 61 66 c3 a9`
- `http://example.com/<F0 9F 98 80>` => 1 segment, exactly `f0 9f 98 80`
- `http://example.com/<E9>` (lone invalid byte) => 1 segment, 1 byte; no replacement char
- a single segment containing all 128 bytes 0x80..0xFF concatenated round-trips byte-for-byte
- a 5000-byte segment of 0xFF round-trips byte-for-byte (5000 bytes out)
- Unicode lookalikes are NOT delimiters: U+FF0F FULLWIDTH SOLIDUS in a segment does not split it
- Unicode/UTF-8 whitespace is not trimmed and not dropped: NBSP (C2 A0), U+2028, U+3000 are
  ordinary segment bytes (`http://example.com/<E3 80 80>/x` => 2 segments)
- percent-escapes survive literally: `/%C3%A9%2F%2E%2E` => 1 segment `"%C3%A9%2F%2E%2E"`
- the ONLY bytes that fail to appear verbatim in a segment are 0x23 '#', 0x2F '/', 0x3F '?'
- byte pairs where a "trail byte" is itself a delimiter behave byte-wise, e.g.
  `http://example.com/<81>/<81>/` => 2 segments each the single byte 0x81;
  `http://e<C3><3A>80/a` => host `"e<C3>"` invalid, port 80 valid => `1 1 0 1 1 [a]`

`to_lower` (the `(unsigned char)` lambda) is never invoked on the driver's path;
`url_encode`/`url_decode` are never invoked either.

### D.6 Robustness (CONFIRMED)

Zero crashes and exit code 0 on all 768 high-byte probes across six structural positions;
stdout is 8-bit clean.

## PART E — LINE 1 hypothesis: CONFIRMED

`is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())` after parsing. Held on every probe,
including the high-byte edges: for all 128 bytes 0x80-0xFF,
`http://<B>` => 1 (host non-empty, LINE3=0), `http://@<B>` => 1, `http://<B>@` => **0**
(userinfo=`<B>`, host and path empty), `<B>://` => 0, `<B>` alone => 1,
`http://?<B>` => 0, `http://#<B>` => 0, `http://:<B>` => 0, `http://[::<B>]` => 1.

## REMAINING UNCERTAINTIES

- 0x00 (NUL) is still untestable through argv.
- Whether trim() is called on the port substring, on query()/fragment(), or on authority()
  remains undecidable through this driver.
- The trim() character set is an image-read fact (offset 53432), not a behavioural one; it is
  independently re-verified but still unreachable from the five printed lines.

Ran roughly 6,100 probes (all counted below actually executed against /workspace/dataset/test16_executable; every reported counterexample was run verbatim and its output pasted).

Sweep inventory: all 128 bytes 0x80-0xFF in 30+ distinct structural positions (mid-host, first host byte, last host byte, host alone, inside brackets with and without a preceding colon, unterminated bracket, userinfo, userinfo+host, scheme first/mid/last char, port pre-digit/mid-digit/post-digit, query value, query key, fragment, fragment with slashes, path segment start/end/lone, whole argument); full 1..255 sweeps at mid-host, non-first scheme position, and whole-argument; 128x6 exit-code sweep; 30 locale-varied probes; byte-exact od comparisons for 128x3 path positions plus a 5000-byte and a 128-byte-concatenation segment.

WHAT SURVIVED THE ATTACK (genuinely solid parts of the rule):
- The host allowed byte set is exactly A-Za-z0-9-.[] — my independent full 1..255 sweep reproduced it exactly (plus the truncators # / : ? @).
- The scheme allowed set is exactly A-Za-z first, then A-Za-z0-9+-. — reproduced exactly by full 1..255 sweep.
- No locale leakage, no signed-char leakage. I specifically attacked this with LC_ALL/LANG set to C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, en_US.iso88591, POSIX and an invalid locale, targeting both isalnum-style host validation and strtol's locale-dependent isspace skip (NBSP 0xA0 before the digits). Zero variation. This was my best shot at breaking Part D and it failed cleanly.
- Path byte-transparency is airtight, verified with od rather than by eye.
- Part E (LINE1) survived every high-byte edge I could construct.
- Part B's image claim is real: I independently confirmed `20 09 0d 0a 00` at file offset 53432, followed by the other parser literals, and `grep -abo` finds that literal at exactly one offset.

WHAT BROKE (why the verdict is 'corrected', not 'confirmed'):
1. Headline: "Rejection of high bytes holds ... inside brackets http://[<B>]/a" is false in general. The engineer generalised from a single bracket probe that happens to contain no colon. Because parse() truncates the host at the FIRST ':' with zero IPv6 awareness, every realistic IPv6 literal shields its high bytes: http://[::\xff]/x, http://[2001:db8::\xff]/a and http://[::\xc3\xa9]/x all give LINE3=1, for all 128 high bytes. This matters for a reimplementation: an implementer following the old rule would add a bracket-aware host validator and get the wrong answer on both LINE3 and LINE4.
2. As a bonus, this same mechanism explains the "known oddity" the previous rule explicitly declared out of scope and unexplained (http://[::1]:8080/x => port INVALID). It is host="[" and port substring ":1]:8080". No IPv6 code exists in this library.
3. "A high byte after the digits is ignored trailing junk => LINE4=1" is stated as an unconditional implication and fails whenever the leading digits are out of range: :65536\xff, :70000\xff, :99999\xff, :2147483647\xff, :2147483648\xff, :99999999999999999999\xff all give LINE4=0. Control :80\xff gives 1.
4. Silences I resolved and folded in: no percent-decoding before host validation ('%' is simply a rejected host byte, so %41%42 does not become AB); no host length cap (300-byte host valid), so the 400-byte UTF-8 host fails on bytes not length; Unicode digits/signs in the port (fullwidth, Arabic-Indic, superscript, U+2212) all give LINE4=0; UTF-8 BOM prefix invalidates the scheme; '@' matching is authority-bounded so an '@' in the path cannot drag a path high byte into the host; the '@' split is on the FIRST '@'; Unicode lookalike delimiters (U+FF0F) and Unicode whitespace (NBSP, U+2028, U+3000) are ordinary segment bytes.

One harness caveat worth passing on: `"$BIN" "$(printf '\n')"` measures the EMPTY string, not LF, because bash command substitution strips trailing newlines. That artifact briefly made 0x0A look like a counterexample to Part C's whole-argument claim; re-measured with `"$BIN" $'\n'` it is `1 0 0 0 1` exactly as the rule says, so I did NOT report it. Part C is intact.
